walkthroughs.body_html:
Electrons, Waves & Photons — a core area of A-Level Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Electrons, Waves & Photons brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Electrons, Waves & Photons.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: In Einstein's photoelectric equation hf = φ + KEmax, the symbol φ represents:
options: The work function of the metal
The kinetic energy of the photon
The threshold wavelength
The stopping distance

mcqs.q: A current of 2 A flows for 10 s. The charge transferred is:
options: 5 C

mcqs.q: Do electrons travel from the battery to the bulb at nearly the speed of light?
options: No — electrons stay still and protons move instead.
Yes — electrons race around the circuit at light speed.
Yes — the current evaporates as light.
No — electron drift velocity is tiny (around mm/s); it is the electric field that is established quickly.

mcqs.q: Is current used up as it passes through a bulb?
options: Yes — the bulb consumes some of the current.
Yes — the current evaporates as light.
No — the current is the same on both sides of the bulb; energy, not charge, is transferred.
No — electrons stay still and protons move instead.

mcqs.q: Does doubling the light intensity increase each photoelectron's maximum kinetic energy?
options: No — electrons stay still and protons move instead.
Yes — intensity raises the work function.
No — it increases the number emitted per second; KEmax depends only on frequency and the work function.
Yes — more intense light produces faster electrons.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Progressive wave”?
options: A wave that transfers energy without transferring matter, described by its amplitude, wavelength and frequency.
The opposition to current flow, R = V/I, measured in ohms.
A quantum of electromagnetic energy, E = hf; photon energies are often quoted in electronvolts.
The rate of flow of electric charge, I = ΔQ/Δt, measured in amperes.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Electric current”?
options: The rate of flow of electric charge, I = ΔQ/Δt, measured in amperes.
The opposition to current flow, R = V/I, measured in ohms.
Emission of electrons from a metal illuminated above its threshold frequency, explained by Einstein's photon model.
A quantum of electromagnetic energy, E = hf; photon energies are often quoted in electronvolts.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Potential difference”?
options: The opposition to current flow, R = V/I, measured in ohms.
Emission of electrons from a metal illuminated above its threshold frequency, explained by Einstein's photon model.
A wave that transfers energy without transferring matter, described by its amplitude, wavelength and frequency.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points, V = W/Q, measured in volts.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Photon”?
options: The rate of flow of electric charge, I = ΔQ/Δt, measured in amperes.
A quantum of electromagnetic energy, E = hf; photon energies are often quoted in electronvolts.
Emission of electrons from a metal illuminated above its threshold frequency, explained by Einstein's photon model.
The opposition to current flow, R = V/I, measured in ohms.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Photoelectric effect”?
options: The opposition to current flow, R = V/I, measured in ohms.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points, V = W/Q, measured in volts.
Emission of electrons from a metal illuminated above its threshold frequency, explained by Einstein's photon model.
A wave that transfers energy without transferring matter, described by its amplitude, wavelength and frequency.

options: Emission of electrons from a metal illuminated above its threshold frequency, explained by Einstein's photon model.
A quantum of electromagnetic energy, E = hf; photon energies are often quoted in electronvolts.
The opposition to current flow, R = V/I, measured in ohms.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points, V = W/Q, measured in volts.
